title: Ifa and the Secret-Keeper
subtitle: Divination in Ellis's survey, beside a legend of a soothsayer

learningObjectives.text: According to Ellis, why is Ifa called the God of Palm Nuts?
In Ogumefu's legend, why do people begin seeking Orisa Oko's advice?

ifa.work: The Yoruba-Speaking Peoples of the Slave Coast of West Africa
ifa.author: A. B. Ellis
ifa.translator: not applicable; authored in English by A. B. Ellis
ifa.locator: Chapter II · CHIEF GODS; Chapter II · CHIEF GODS, normalized characters 34980-35520
ifa.excerpt: Ifa, god of divination, who is usually termed the God of Palm Nuts, because sixteen palm-nuts are used in the process of divination, comes after Shango in order of eminence. The name Ifa apparently means something scraped or wiped off: he has the title of Gbangba (explanation, demonstration, proof). Ifa's secondary attribute is to cause fecundity: he presides at births, and women pray to him to be made fruitful; while on this account offerings are always made to him before marriage, it being considered a disgrace not to bear children.
ifa.note: Verbatim English text from Ellis's 1894 survey of the Yoruba-speaking peoples. It is colonial-era ethnography: claims belong to Ellis's report, and his comparative and evolutionary framing is commentary, not community testimony.

babalawo.work: The Yoruba-Speaking Peoples of the Slave Coast of West Africa
babalawo.author: A. B. Ellis
babalawo.translator: not applicable; authored in English by A. B. Ellis
babalawo.locator: Chapter V · PRIESTS AND WORSHIP; Chapter V · PRIESTS AND WORSHIP, normalized characters 5363-5805
babalawo.excerpt: The reason of the Babalawo taking the highest place in the priesthood is that it is through his agency, as the priest of Ifa, the god of divination, that man learns what is necessary to be done to please the other gods. The priests of Ifa thus, to a certain extent, control and direct the worship of the other gods, and in time of calamity, war, or pestilence it is their business to declare what ought to be done to make the gods propitious.
babalawo.note: Verbatim English text from Ellis's 1894 survey of the Yoruba-speaking peoples. It is colonial-era ethnography: claims belong to Ellis's report, and his comparative and evolutionary framing is commentary, not community testimony.

orisa-oko.author: Yoruba storytellers; collected and published in English by M. I. Ogumefu
orisa-oko.translator: not applicable; authored in English by M. I. Ogumefu
orisa-oko.locator: Legend IX · ORISA OKO; Legend IX · ORISA OKO, normalized characters 271-850
orisa-oko.excerpt: He earned a meagre living by trapping in his nets guinea-fowls on the land of rich farmers, but because of his solitary life and his habit of silence, he was respected as a man possessed of secret knowledge which he did not care to divulge. As years went by, he grew too old for hunting, and took up his residence in a cave. People now thought him more mysterious than ever, and came to him for advice about the future, so that in a short time he won great renown as a soothsayer. From far and near people came to consult him, and in this way he managed to live very comfortably.
orisa-oko.note: Verbatim English text from M. I. Ogumefu's 1929 collection, which his preface describes as belonging to the Yoruba country of Southern Nigeria. It is a Yoruba-authored retelling for readers, not an ethnographic record of practice.

narrativeBlocks.title: A god of palm nuts
narrativeBlocks.body: In Ellis's 1894 survey, Ifa is the god of divination, usually called the God of Palm Nuts because sixteen palm-nuts are used in the divination process.

narrativeBlocks.title: The highest priesthood
narrativeBlocks.body: Source quotation (The Yoruba-Speaking Peoples of the Slave Coast of West Africa; whitespace normalized): “The reason of the Babalawo taking the highest place in the priesthood is that it is through his agency, as the priest of Ifa, the god of divination, that man learns what is necessary to be done to please the other gods. The priests of Ifa thus, to a certain extent, control and direct the worship of the other gods, and in time of calamity, war, or pestilence it is their business to declare what ought to be done to make the gods propitious.”

narrativeBlocks.title: Why the Babalawo outrank
narrativeBlocks.body: Ellis says the Babalawo, priests of Ifa, hold the highest place in the priesthood because through Ifa people learn what must be done to please the other gods. Other priests divine too, but without Ifa's palm-nuts and board.

narrativeBlocks.title: A legend about a soothsayer
narrativeBlocks.body: Ogumefu retells how Orisa Oko, a solitary hunter, gained fame when people mistook his silence for secret knowledge. It is a story about a reputation for seeing the future, not a description of Ifa practice.

narrativeBlocks.title: Report versus legend
narrativeBlocks.body: Ellis describes an institution: priests, palm-nuts, a board, ranks. Ogumefu tells a tale about one man credited with foresight. Both involve divination; they are different kinds of evidence.
